transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-09 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Jules Park (Redwood SRE); Lena Ortiz, Tom Briggs, Aisha Khan, Ben Cho (RiverMark)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — go over last weeks bench, talk TTFT targets, streaming results, kernel choices, and agree next steps.
[00:18] Lena Ortiz: thanks Maya, yep we have a hard deadline to show 50ms median and sub-200ms p95 on our short form flows by end of month.
[00:30] Carlos Rivera: cool, so we ran the microbench on our staging cluster, same model variant you guys onboarded — we tested both streaming and non-streaming, and did different kernel selections. initial notes — streaming helps TTFT a lot for short sequences, like 8-32 tokens.
[00:45] Tom Briggs: can you quantify "a lot" — like what numbers should we expect at our target 200ms p95?
[00:52] Carlos Rivera: sure, on our staging hw (A100-ish fleet sim) we saw median TTFT go from ~85ms non-streaming down to ~55ms streaming for 16-token responses, p95 improved from ~210ms to ~170ms. caveats — network egress and SNI handshake adds variability, so your VPC peering numbers will matter.
[01:18] Aisha Khan: that aligns with what we saw in the first pilot. but Ben saw some spikes when sequence length jumped to 128 tokens.
[01:25] Ben Cho: yeah some queries expand, we have tail cases where users ask follow-ups. our distribution is 70% <=32 tokens, 25% 33-128, 5% >128.
[01:40] Carlos Rivera: okay couple levers then: streaming reduces TTFT because we flush partial frames earlier; batching policy needs to be sequence-length-aware so short sequences don't wait on long ones; kernel selection matters for long seqs.
[02:00] Jules Park: we also noticed KV cache warmup — first call cold KV cache can add ~30-40ms if cache miss; prefix caching helps for repeated contexts, but cold-start work remains.
[02:15] Lena Ortiz: is KV cache persistent between requests in Redwood Dedicated? we need persistence across sessions for some user flows.
[02:22] Maya Chen: yes, in Dedicated the KV cache persists for the worker lifetime; for Private you can tune eviction. caveat — very long-lived caches increase memory footprint.
[02:37] Tom Briggs: about kernels — you mentioned auto picking vs force cuBLAS — which one did you run for the bench?
[02:45] Carlos Rivera: we used kernel=auto initially. for seq<64 auto picked lighter optimized kernels that favor latency. for seq>128 it picked matmul-heavy kernels (cuBLAS-like). we also ran a manual Triton-style kernel path which reduced p99 for long seq by 8-10% but slightly increased median for short seq.
[03:10] Maya Chen: to be clear, "auto" is generally safest — runtime chooses kernel by sample latency profiles. but if you know your distribution, pinning can help.
[03:22] Ben Cho: any quantization changes here? we had concerns about accuracy vs latency.
[03:28] Carlos Rivera: we tested 4-bit QLoRA-like quant and int8 on some paths. int8 saved ~15% latency on heavy ops but introduced occasional tokenization artifacts — we logged a 0.8% drop in exact-match on our eval set. recommended: keep fp16 for now for quality, test hybrid quant on tails.
[03:55] Aisha Khan: about streaming implementation — does Redwood stream SSE or gRPC chunked responses? our infra prefers gRPC.
[04:05] Maya Chen: Redwood supports both; current staging bench used HTTP chunked by default, but we can enable gRPC streaming for your test. small note — some proxies (we saw with bedrock-proxy setups) buffer chunked responses so end-to-end matters.
[04:25] Tom Briggs: network variability — our egress bandwidth is 1Gb with bursts to 5Gb, could that cause jitter in TTFT?
[04:32] Carlos Rivera: yes, especially if you have TLS handshake on first byte. we recommend keep-alive and connection pooling from your side. TTL for sockets and long-lived connections on Dedicated helps.
[04:48] Lena Ortiz: earlier you mentioned batching policies — can you explain the sequence-aware batching again?
[04:55] Carlos Rivera: sure — rather than batch strictly by arrival time, runtime groups by expected output length bucket and latency SLO. short seqs get small micro-batches with aggressive timer; long seqs wait to fill bigger batches. this reduces head-of-line blocking. we can share the config we used.
[05:20] Ben Cho: any impact on throughput? if we split batches by length don't we lose some overall throughput?
[05:27] Jules Park: minor throughput tradeoff but big latency wins on p95 for short seqs. the runtime compensates with dynamic scaling.
[05:35] Tom Briggs: regarding your claim streaming lowers TTFT by 30ms — is that independent of tokenization overhead? sometimes tokenization causes split tokens and extra model steps.
[05:46] Carlos Rivera: good point — we included tokenization cost in the bench; streaming's gain is primarily post-tokenization: early emit of logits reduces time-to-first-token. if you have complex on-client tokenization, send pre-tokenized requests to save ~10-15ms.
[06:03] Lena Ortiz: we will try pre-tokenizing in the next test.
[06:07] Maya Chen: quick recap on numbers we saw: median TTFT 55ms streaming for 16 tokens, non-streaming 85ms; p95 streaming ~170ms, p95 non-streaming ~210ms. for 128 tokens p95 rises to ~450ms non-streaming, streaming helped reduce by ~30-40ms but longer seq dominates compute.
[06:30] Aisha Khan: what about cold-starts when autoscaling adds workers?
[06:36] Jules Park: our scaling cold-start measured ~700-900ms for new worker spin and model load in default config; with warm-pools we can tighten to ~250-300ms. Dedicated offers reserved pool option which is what we suggest for strict SLOs.
[06:52] Tom Briggs: reserved pool will cost more — can we do burst + warm pool hybrid?
[06:57] Carlos Rivera: yes, hybrid is common — small reserved baseline + autoscale for bursts. also partial model residency helps if you have multiple model variants.
[07:10] Ben Cho: kernel tuning — is there a config we can tweak at runtime or does it require redeploy?
[07:15] Carlos Rivera: kernel selection is hot-swappable at runtime via the console; we can push canary kernel changes to a subset of workers and measure. no full redeploy needed. caveat: some kernels require CUDA driver compat, but those are mostly supported.
[07:30] Maya Chen: action item: Redwood to run 1k QPS bench with streaming enabled and kernel=auto, and also try kernel=pinned for long seqs, report p50/p95/p99 and cpu/gpu util.
[07:44] Lena Ortiz: will you include tokenization breakdown and top 5 latency contributors?
[07:49] Carlos Rivera: yes. we'll include a flame graph and per-stage timing.
[07:56] Aisha Khan: about instrumentation — can we push custom tracing headers so we can join traces in our APM?
[08:01] Jules Park: yes, Redwood supports trace propagation (W3C traceparent header). include that in the bench and we can correlate traces.
[08:12] Tom Briggs: security question — we need SOC2 docs and network diagrams for procurement.
[08:17] Maya Chen: I'll send SOC2, ISO artifacts and network diagram. Tom I'll CC you.
[08:24] Ben Cho: small nit — in previous transcript you referenced KV cache as "K V cache" and sometimes "KVc ache" — sorry bad joke — but please clarify caching semantics in the doc.
[08:33] Carlos Rivera: noted, we'll include a clear table: warm vs cold semantics, eviction policies, memory footprint per model.
[08:42] Lena Ortiz: about canary rollouts — we want automatic fallback to a smaller model if latency SLO is breached. is that supported?
[08:50] Carlos Rivera: yes, Redwood's routing policy can do latency-based fallback to a compatible smaller variant; we can set thresholds and cool-down windows. we tested an A/B where requests over 300ms rerouted to smaller model and quality drop was minimal for diagnostic flows.
[09:10] Maya Chen: any blockers from RiverMark side?
[09:14] Tom Briggs: main blocker is our peering egress throttles and procurement docs. once we have SOC2 + network diagrams and do the 1k bench I'll be comfortable moving to reserved baseline.
[09:25] Lena Ortiz: quality validation after any quantization or kernel change is non-negotiable for us — we need the eval harness run and a report.
[09:33] Carlos Rivera: agreed — we'll run your 1k eval prompts and provide diff metrics.
[09:38] Maya Chen: perfect. let's capture next steps — Carlos will run bench, Maya will send security docs, Tom to send peering logs, Lena to validate quality after change.
[09:51] Ben Cho: one question — is there an easy toggle to pre-tokenize at client side in your SDK?
[09:57] Carlos Rivera: yes, SDKs have pre-tokenize utilities; we'll add sample code in the repo we share.
[10:05] Maya Chen: ok final recap and timeline: Redwood to share tuned config and bench results by 2027-03-12; RiverMark to provide traces and peering info by 2027-03-11; schedule integrated bench 2027-03-15. any objections?
[10:20] Tom Briggs: none.
[10:22] Lena Ortiz: sounds good.
[10:25] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
[10:30] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: some words may be imperfect — product names like "Redwood Dedicated" occasionally transcribed as "Redwood Dedicatd" or "Redwood Dedi". acronyms (KV cache, VPC, SSO) sometimes rendered inconsistently.
